en: In the Mak-Ban geothermal plant, magma heats underground water into steam, which then spins turbines to generate electricity for Luzon.
Slightly acidic rainwater slowly dissolves the limestone bedrock in Puerto Princesa, carving out massive underground cave systems over thousands of years.
Tiny coral polyps in the Tubbataha Reefs extract calcium carbonate from seawater to build hard skeletons, gradually forming massive, complex reef structures.
The temperature difference between the Asian landmass and the Pacific Ocean causes air to move, creating the seasonal Amihan and Habagat monsoon winds.
At Maria Cristina Falls, the Agus River flows over hard basalt above softer rock, which erodes faster to create the steep vertical drop.
As the Cagayan River reaches the calm Babuyan Channel, it slows down and deposits carried sediments to form a large river delta.
Warm ocean waters in the Philippine Sea evaporate rapidly, releasing latent heat that powers and intensifies approaching typhoons before they hit land.
Repeated underwater volcanic eruptions in Camiguin eject lava that cools and accumulates above sea level, gradually building new volcanic landforms and islands.
The dense, tangled root systems of mangrove forests in Panguil Bay trap moving water and sediments, reducing coastal erosion during strong storm surges.
Rainwater seeps deep into fractures near Mount Makiling, gets heated by underlying magma, and rises back to the surface as natural hot springs.
Weathering of volcanic ash from Mayon Volcano breaks down into fine minerals, mixing with organic matter to create highly fertile agricultural soil in Albay.
The gravitational pull of the moon and sun pulls the ocean waters of Manila Bay, causing the water level to regularly rise and fall.
